title: Choose your company
hook: pick friends who are calm, since moods are catching (On Tranquility 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday: serve where you can, when the big stage is closed. Your line was serve where i can. Did the small private thing get done? Day four hundred ninety-eight.

Someone walks into the office in a foul mood, and within twenty minutes three other people are snapping too. Or the opposite: a friend who's simply easy to be around, and you notice your shoulders drop the moment they sit down. You didn't decide either thing. It just spread. Modern psychologists have a name for this: emotional contagion. Seneca didn't have the name, but he had the observation. In chapter seven of On Tranquility, after work and service, he turns to the people we spend our days with, and gives some very practical advice. Today: choose your company.
screen: `ONE FOUL MOOD, THREE SNAPPING.` → `ONE EASY FRIEND, SHOULDERS DROP.` → `IT SPREADS.`

segments.voice: First, the gift of a friend. Nothing, Seneca says, delights the mind like a faithful friendship: someone you can tell a secret to as safely as telling yourself, whose talk eases your worry and whose advice helps you decide. He's not cynical about people. He wants you to have friends. Second, choose with care. Vices spread, he warns, by contact. They pass to whoever is closest, the way an illness passes to those who sit by the sick bed. So pick, as far as you can, people who aren't ruled by their passions: not the rage-prone, not the greedy, not the one always in a panic. Third, don't wait for a saint. Seneca adds a realistic note. Don't go looking for a perfectly wise friend; people have searched for centuries. Choose the least bad. Steadiness, not perfection. Fourth, beware the moaner. The friend Seneca singles out is the one who's always gloomy, who complains about everything and finds a grievance in every piece of news. Even if they're loyal and kind, he says, a companion who's constantly upset is an enemy to your calm. Fair note: this isn't advice to abandon a friend who's grieving or ill. Seneca is talking about the mood we keep company with by habit, not the person who needs us right now. And it cuts both ways. If calm is catching, then so are you. Somebody is choosing your company too.
screen: `NOTHING DELIGHTS LIKE A FAITHFUL FRIEND.` · `VICES SPREAD BY CONTACT.` · `CHOOSE THE LEAST BAD.` · `BEWARE THE CONSTANT MOANER.` · then, large: `CALM IS CATCHING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the five people you spend the most time with, in person or on a screen. Picture each face for a breath. With each one, notice what your body does: does it settle, or tighten? No judging them. Just noticing. Now pick the one who settles you most. Picture sitting with them. Let some of their steadiness reach you now. Then ask: when people sit with me, what do they catch? The bell holds the time.
Choose your company. Seneca's advice in On Tranquility: moods and vices spread by contact, so keep close to the steady. Today's word.
Your line: calm is catching. Spend some time today with the steady person you pictured, even ten minutes or a call. And try to be someone worth catching. Day four hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: People who follow Seneca's advice pay attention to how the company they keep affects their mood, and seek out steady, calm friends.

fork.setup: you have a loyal, kind friend who complains about everything, every time you meet. what would Seneca say?
options: a constant moaner is an enemy to your calm.
fork.reveal: he names the always-gloomy companion, however loyal, as a threat to tranquility, and tells you to choose company with care.

original.note: Latin, 'friendship': which Seneca says delights the mind more than anything.

trapdoor: what you thought: choosing friends by mood sounds cold.
what it means: moods spread by contact, so Seneca says keep close to the steady, and be steady for others.
what a scholar hears: Seneca's contagion image is medical; ancient medicine already knew some illnesses passed to those nursing the sick, and he applies it to the soul.

notes: On Tranquility 7 paraphrased: faithful friendship delights the mind (secrets told as safely as to oneself); choose those free of passions; vices spread by contact like disease; don't seek the wise man, choose the least bad; avoid the gloomy complainer. Confirm.
'Emotional contagion' is a modern psychology term (Hatfield and colleagues); the script only names it, making no scientific claim. Confirm acceptable.
Fairness note about grieving friends is the path's own framing.
